rows.title: Brisbane City Council

options.name: Madison Davis
options.description: Incumbent. Detailed platform covers downtown maintenance, vacant storefronts, childcare, fiscal repairs and data-center restrictions. Expanded record above.
options.why: Incumbency and first-place finish in 2022 are the strongest verified electoral signals in this field. Five candidates compete for two seats, so she is favored rather than assured.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The city biography records council service since 2015, prior Parks & Recreation Commission service and two years as mayor. It also lists Chamber president/CEO and ownership of Furnish, a staging/interior-design business.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Her experience is directly in city government. The city’s audit update documents overdue financial reports and internal-control weaknesses during her tenure; those are collective oversight issues, not proof of personal wrongdoing.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: A city-hosted biography confirms listed roles; it is not an independent evaluation of performance. See the detailed profile above for the housing-compliance letter, recusal and campaign proposals.

options.name: Julie Sims
options.description: Parks & Recreation commissioner and business owner. Supports open-space protection, community programs and prohibiting large data centers.
options.why: Five-plus years of commission service and campaign-listed backing from councilmembers Frank Kern and Coleen Mackin support an organization advantage among challengers.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: City records confirm appointment to Parks & Recreation in February 2021 and reappointment in February 2025. YouthPoint Health describes reporting for the Half Moon Bay Review, district-office work for Quentin Kopp, communications leadership at Robert Half and a 2017 move to Room to Read. Fortitude Careers independently lists her on its board.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: This establishes a broader communications and nonprofit career, plus sustained city-commission service. Her commission assignments cover parks concerts, habitat restoration, public art, recreation, seniors and youth.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: Commission and nonprofit service are relevant experience, but do not establish success managing a city budget. The reviewed sources do not provide an audited record of her individual program outcomes.

options.name: Christopher Hornick
options.description: Business leader. Supports Baylands and Quarry development with safeguards, downtown investment and recreation facilities.
options.why: A development-focused platform establishes a serious candidacy. The expanded forum review adds accountability proposals, but supplies no new polling or vote-intention evidence; this remains a weak prior.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: His public disclosure identifies interests in HBS Consulting and HBSC Strategic Services. HBSC’s management page describes him as founder, an adviser to executives and an interim CFO/COO/CIO, with Rutgers, computer-science graduate and Columbia MBA credentials.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: The firm’s account describes finance, operations and technology-transformation experience. It is a more specific professional record than “business leader,” but comes from his own firm.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: The filing corroborates business ties, not client results or academic degrees. No municipal executive track record or independent audit of those claimed business outcomes was established.

options.name: Charles Spencer
options.description: Business owner and former nonprofit CFO. Emphasizes fiscal oversight, transparency, city finances and data-center concerns.
options.why: Financial credentials and an active campaign establish a plausible challenger. The reviewed evidence does not establish an electoral advantage over Davis or Sims; this is a weak prior.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: His filed candidate statement describes a small-business owner and former nonprofit CFO. The wider search did not establish the nonprofit employer, duration or audited outcomes of that CFO role.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Fiscal scrutiny and transparency are campaign priorities. A CFO title is potentially relevant, but the underlying institution and responsibilities need verification before it can be treated as evidence of delivery.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: People with the same name in other countries and industries were excluded. Lack of corroboration here is an unresolved research gap, not proof that the claim is false.

options.name: Chaya-Bella David
options.description: Community volunteer and returning candidate. Her official statement emphasizes community service and youth participation.
options.why: Finished fifth of five in the three-seat 2024 race with 615 candidate votes. That is a demonstrated base, but below the 995 votes of the last winner; the 2026 field is different.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The city’s 2019 volunteer-recognition page names Chaya-Bella David. Her filed statement describes community volunteering; the reviewed 2024 election record shows a previous council run.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: The public evidence establishes civic participation. It does not establish a record administering municipal budgets or approving major land-use projects.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: No independently corroborated degree or detailed employment history was established in this review. Sparse evidence should not be turned into either a personal attack or a conclusion about her ability.

rows.method: Two-seat subjective strength model; no local poll. Weights Davis 5, Sims 3, Hornick 1.5, Spencer 1, David 0.6. Plackett–Luce top-two inclusion gives 75.8%, 57.6%, 31.7%, 21.7%, 13.2%; display is coarsened to 75/60/30/20/15. Assumed strengths are judgments, not fitted parameters. Sensitivity bands below are judgment ranges, not confidence intervals.
rows.office: Two seats on the city’s governing council. Council sets local policy and budgets and decides land-use applications; staff implement those decisions.
rows.decision: Read the project explanations and candidate backgrounds above. Compare specific decisions, public records and conflicts of interest, rather than treating an endorsement or a win forecast as a recommendation.

rows.title: County Supervisor · District 5

options.name: Mark Nagales
options.description: South San Francisco vice mayor. Campaign emphasizes housing, childcare, public services and transportation.
options.why: Campaign lists support from three sitting county supervisors and several unions and media organizations. This earns only a small edge against another established local officeholder.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: South San Francisco councilmember, elected in 2018 and mayor in 2022, according to Bay Area News Group reporting.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Supports an Article 34 authorization approach to public low-income housing and stronger tenant protections; says he will pursue recovery of missing state vehicle-license-fee revenue.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: The article corroborates officeholding and reports proposals. It is not a causal audit of housing outcomes or a district-wide poll.

options.name: Juslyn Cabrera Manalo
options.description: Daly City councilmember. Campaign emphasizes affordability, healthcare and working families.
options.why: Strong elected-office record and a citywide Daly City base keep this close. She won 23,477 candidate votes in 2024; citywide and ward totals are not directly comparable.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: Daly City councilmember first elected in 2016, with mayoral terms in 2018, 2021 and 2024, according to Bay Area News Group.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Points to Midway Village housing work; proposes using county land and outside funding for affordable housing and state relationships to recover missing revenue.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: The record and proposals deserve comparison, but project-level credit and future funding are not guaranteed.

rows.method: Subjective 55–45 assessment from officeholding, prior results and campaign-reported endorsements. No district-wide poll or campaign-finance audit was available in this review. October 13–14 independent reporting adds records and financing context, but does not validate the 55–45 split.
rows.office: One seat representing northern San Mateo County. County decisions affect health and social services, housing resources and the budget; they are separate from Brisbane City Council decisions.
rows.decision: Both candidates have municipal experience. Compare housing implementation and the response to missing state vehicle-license-fee revenue. Their citywide and district election totals are not comparable measures of countywide support.

rows.title: Brisbane School District board

options.name: Sarah Duffy
options.description: Incumbent school board member.
options.why: An incumbency-only prior favors existing officeholders. No candidate-specific polling or comparative performance evaluation was found.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The school district’s own roster identifies Duffy as current board president with a term ending December 2026.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: That is direct governing experience. KQED received no policy questionnaire response from her.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: Her broader professional qualifications and individual votes on budgets, contracts and student outcomes were not established by the reviewed roster.

options.name: Morgan Finlay
options.description: Appointed incumbent school board member.
options.why: Incumbency provides a modest name-recognition prior; appointment is not proof of electoral support.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The district’s roster identifies Finlay as a current trustee with a December 2026 term end. KQED identifies an appointed incumbent.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Current board service is verified. KQED received no policy questionnaire response.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: Appointment is not evidence of electoral support. The district profile did not supply a career biography or a comparative performance record.

options.name: Charlene Larson
options.description: Ballot designation: retired federal employee.
options.why: Three seats for four candidates creates a high baseline chance. With no better electoral data, this estimate gives newcomers equal strength.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The candidate roster and KQED list Larson as a retired federal employee. That designation does not identify an agency, job or years of service.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: KQED received no policy questionnaire response from Larson.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: No independently verified detailed federal-employment history or comparative school-governance record was established. The absence of a questionnaire response does not imply any particular policy position.

options.name: Emily Wirowek
options.description: Ballot designation: parent / attorney.
options.why: Same newcomer prior as Larson. This forecast does not evaluate qualifications or imply a preference between them.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The State Bar lists Emily Amber Wirowek, license 264993, as active, with Wirowek Law Group in Brisbane. This independently verifies the attorney credential.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: KQED reports support for classroom-phone restrictions, school resource officers and new charter schools; opposition to school closures and to the proposed teacher-misconduct database. These are candidate responses, not voting records.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: An active law license does not establish education-policy expertise or an education-results record. Her questionnaire offers more policy detail than the other responses received, not proof she is more qualified.

rows.method: Three-seat Plackett–Luce prior: incumbent weights 1.4 each, newcomer weights 1 each. Inclusion probabilities 81/81/69/69, coarsened to 80/80/70/70. No polling; no school-policy recommendation. Arithmetic audit: 80 + 80 + 70 + 70 = 300%, equal to three seats × 100%. These are overlapping chances of inclusion, not mutually exclusive outcomes. Four identical 80% chances would total 320% and would be inconsistent here.
rows.office: Choose up to three of four candidates, if you live in this school district. The board oversees the superintendent, school budget, facilities and labor contracts.
rows.decision: Compare stewardship of the district with concrete positions on school closures, classroom phones and charter schools. KQED received policy responses from Wirowek but not the other three; nonresponse is a gap, not a position.

rows.title: Insurance Commissioner

options.name: Ben Allen
options.description: Democratic state senator.
options.why: Probolsky’s Oct 26 release reports Allen 25%, Kim 21%, with 54% unsure. The small lead warrants a modest edge, heavily discounted for undecided voters and conflicting earlier signals.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: State senator since 2014. Independent reporting identifies recently signed legislation on insurance enforcement, home hardening and nonrenewal notice.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Favors improving the private market and wildfire resilience. CalMatters reports industry-linked outside spending supporting him; he said he did not seek or welcome it.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: Outside spending is separate from direct campaign donations. The article does not establish illegal coordination or regulatory capture.

options.name: Jane Kim
options.description: Democratic attorney / consumer advocate; former SF supervisor.
options.why: The same poll leaves most voters undecided, so this is still competitive. A four-point stated-preference deficit is not a 60–40 vote-share forecast.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: Former San Francisco supervisor; later worked for the Working Families Party. Independent reporting identifies tenant, wage and community-college policy work.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Proposes a publicly administered disaster-insurance layer. CalMatters reports outside support from the Working Families Party, her former employer.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: A public-insurance proposal is not an enacted or fully costed program. Funding, coverage and exposure to catastrophic losses remain central implementation questions.

rows.method: Subjective 60–40 win forecast from the latest verified public poll; undecided voters and poll uncertainty dominate. No full multi-poll model was fitted.
rows.office: The commissioner regulates property and casualty insurance rates and investigates insurer practices. This affects home, renter and auto coverage as well as wildfire recovery.
rows.decision: The central choice is between stabilizing and enforcing the private-insurance system and creating a public disaster-insurance layer. Compare implementation, affordability and who ultimately bears catastrophic losses.

rows.title: Board of Equalization · District 2

options.name: Sally J. Lieber
options.description: Democrat; incumbent board member.
options.why: Original 60% judgment estimate retained. San Francisco’s certified June primary gave Lieber 71.59% and Pimentel 14.23%, but this is only one part of the district and a multi-candidate primary. It cannot be converted directly into a November win probability.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The BOE biography records Mountain View council and mayoral service, election to the Assembly in 2002 and election to the BOE in 2022.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Supports keeping the board as an elected forum for taxpayers; CalMatters reports her defense of its current role after the 2017 removal of many functions.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: A long legislative résumé is not itself evidence of accurate tax administration. No current head-to-head poll or comparative service-quality audit was verified.

options.name: John Pimentel
options.description: Democrat; community-college district trustee.
options.why: Original complementary 40% estimate retained. The verified San Francisco primary result is not district-wide or a head-to-head poll. New background evidence does not justify pretending the original estimate is calibrated.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: The college district’s historical biography records renewable-energy businesses, Bain consulting, 1990s state transportation work and election to its board in 2020. It lists Berkeley and Harvard Business School education.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Argues for reform; the pro-Pimentel GrowSF endorsement specifically supports his willingness to eliminate the office. Read it as advocacy, alongside the BOE’s own account of its duties.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: The district biography is historical and says its term expires in 2024; it does not alone verify current officeholding. Business outcomes in a biography are not an independent audit, and abolition requires action beyond one member.

rows.method: Incumbency-only judgment prior in a same-party race. Evidence is especially limited. Background research expanded October 27; no newly verified general-election poll supports recalibrating these numbers.
rows.office: The Board of Equalization oversees county property-assessment practices and directly values certain utility and railroad property. It is not the Legislature and does not set everyone’s tax rate.
rows.decision: Compare maintaining an elected taxpayer forum with restructuring or abolishing the board. A member cannot abolish this constitutionally created office alone. The dispute is about tax administration and institutional design, not a broad mandate to rewrite tax law.

rows.title: Superintendent of Public Instruction

options.name: Richard Barrera
options.description: Ballot designation: state superintendent advisor.
options.why: A broad Democratic-aligned statewide prior favors Barrera, but this is a nonpartisan ballot and no current head-to-head poll was verified. Consequently the upset tail is larger.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: CalMatters identifies Barrera as San Diego Unified board president.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Emphasizes school funding, early-childhood education and teacher recruitment.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: The retained 90% estimate is a political-alignment prior, not a measured assessment of either candidate’s school performance.

options.name: Sonja Shaw
options.description: Ballot designation: school district president.
options.why: A credible upset tail remains in a lower-information nonpartisan contest. This estimate is prior-driven, not measured voter support.

evidence.label: Background & qualifications
evidence.text: CalMatters identifies Shaw as Chino Valley board president.

evidence.label: Record & policy difference
evidence.text: Her record includes opposition to transgender-student protections; she emphasizes academic basics and parental authority.

evidence.label: What remains uncertain
evidence.text: The office’s reduced 2027 powers limit what either candidate can implement directly.

rows.method: Low-confidence political-alignment prior, not a candidate-performance evaluation or a race-specific poll.
rows.office: A statewide education office with limited control over local districts. CalMatters reports that a 2027 restructuring transfers many duties to a governor-appointed education commissioner and the state school board.
rows.decision: Compare the candidates’ school-board records and education priorities, while recognizing that campaign promises may exceed the office’s new powers.

rows.title: Measure X · business-license tax
rows.method: Estimated $1M additional annual general-fund revenue; removes specified exemptions including nonprofits and rentals under five units. Separate industry taxes remain.

options.name: Yes
options.description: For most businesses: $50 up to $25,000 receipts; then $1 per $1,000 above that. Operating costs can become the tax base.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Estimated $1M additional annual general-fund revenue; removes specified exemptions including nonprofits and rentals under five units. Separate industry taxes remain.

options.name: No
options.description: Keep the existing tiered business-license tax.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Replace most of Brisbane’s tiered business-license taxes with a gross-receipts formula and remove specified exemptions. The city attorney describes this as a general tax: revenue is available for general city services, not a guaranteed dedicated program.
rows.decision: Weigh the city’s estimated $1 million in extra annual revenue against who pays more, including nonprofits and small rental operations losing exemptions. A business’s operating costs can be used as the tax base; this is not a tax on profit.

rows.office: Authorize $11.25 billion in housing bonds: $10 billion for housing programs and $1.25 billion for veteran home loans. The legislative analyst estimates $500–600 million in annual General Fund repayment for about 25 years on the housing-program bonds.
rows.decision: Weigh subsidized housing delivered sooner against long-term repayment and the opportunity cost for other public services.

rows.title: Proposition 2 · Rainy Day Fund
rows.method: Changes reserve capacity and extends required extra debt payments; also changes how reserves interact with the spending limit.

options.name: Yes

options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.decision: Weigh protection against future budget downturns against less money available for services in high-revenue years.

rows.title: Proposition 3 · High-income tax extension
rows.method: Official estimate: maintain $5B–$15B in annual state income-tax revenue. Not a new tax on all earners.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Make the existing high-income tax increase permanent instead of allowing it to expire in 2031.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Official estimate: maintain $5B–$15B in annual state income-tax revenue. Not a new tax on all earners.

options.name: No
options.description: Allow that temporary tax increase to expire in 2031.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Make the existing higher income-tax rates on high earners permanent instead of allowing them to expire in 2031. The analyst estimates annual revenue of roughly $5–15 billion, varying substantially with the economy and stock market.
rows.decision: Weigh continued program funding against permanently extending the tax. Do not confuse this income tax with Proposition 40’s one-time wealth tax.

rows.title: Proposition 4 · Public campaign financing
rows.method: Permits programs rather than creating one universal program. Certain earmarked funds cannot be used.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Allow state and local governments to create public campaign-financing programs, subject to funding restrictions.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Permits programs rather than creating one universal program. Certain earmarked funds cannot be used.

options.name: No
options.description: Keep the prohibition for the state and most local governments.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Allow state and local governments to create public campaign-financing programs. This measure does not itself create or fund one. Costs depend on later choices; state guidance costs are expected to be relatively small.
rows.decision: Weigh the option of publicly financing campaigns against taxpayer costs and the design of safeguards. A Yes vote does not automatically give money to candidates.

options.description: Keep the replacement-candidate question on recall ballots.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Remove the replacement-candidate question from recall ballots. Vacancies would instead be filled under rules involving appointments or special elections, depending on the office and timing. Election costs could rise or fall.
rows.decision: Weigh the replacement process and democratic accountability, including who appoints a successor and when voters get another election.

rows.title: Proposition 37 · New-home loan program
rows.method: Eligible new homes and borrowers face price, income, occupancy and downpayment rules. Official summary estimates no direct state or local cost.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Create homebuying assistance using up to $25B in revenue bonds repaid by borrowers.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Eligible new homes and borrowers face price, income, occupancy and downpayment rules. Official summary estimates no direct state or local cost.

options.name: No
options.description: Do not require creation of the program.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Create a new homebuying-assistance program using up to $25 billion in revenue bonds repaid by participating homeowners. The analyst identifies uncertainty about investor demand, loan pricing and how much new building would result.
rows.decision: Weigh access to purchase financing against borrower costs and uncertain housing-supply effects. These are loans, not free down payments.

rows.title: Proposition 38 · Immunology research bonds
rows.method: Half goes to a specified UC-affiliated nonprofit institute. Estimated debt cost $500M–$600M annually for about 20 years, potentially offset by research revenue.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Authorize $8.4B in general-obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Half goes to a specified UC-affiliated nonprofit institute. Estimated debt cost $500M–$600M annually for about 20 years, potentially offset by research revenue.

options.name: No
options.description: Do not authorize this borrowing.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. The analyst estimates annual General Fund repayment of $500–600 million for about 20 years; commercial discoveries could yield uncertain future revenue.
rows.decision: Weigh potential research benefits against borrowing costs and the possibility that medical or financial returns take decades or do not materialize.

rows.title: Proposition 39 · Voter identification
rows.method: Official annual implementation-cost estimate ranges from tens of millions to low hundreds of millions. Changes the requirements for a ballot to count.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Require government ID for in-person voting and designated ID digits on mailed ballot envelopes.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Official annual implementation-cost estimate ranges from tens of millions to low hundreds of millions. Changes the requirements for a ballot to count.

options.name: No
options.description: Keep the existing signature-based identity process.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Require additional government-issued identification for voting, replacing reliance on signature-based identification alone. The analyst estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars in additional annual costs, depending on implementation.
rows.decision: Weigh the proposed identification requirement against administrative costs and access for eligible voters lacking the required identification.

rows.title: Proposition 40 · One-time billionaire tax
rows.method: Official estimate: temporary revenue in the tens of billions; possible ongoing income-tax revenue reduction below $1B annually. Interacts with Props 41 and 42.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on certain taxpayers with assets above $1B, primarily for healthcare.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Official estimate: temporary revenue in the tens of billions; possible ongoing income-tax revenue reduction below $1B annually. Interacts with Props 41 and 42.

options.name: No
options.description: Do not impose the proposed one-time wealth tax.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on covered billionaires, primarily funding health care. The analyst expects temporary revenue in the tens of billions and a possible ongoing income-tax revenue loss below $1 billion annually.
rows.decision: Weigh temporary public funding against valuation, administration and taxpayer-response risks. Conflicts with Propositions 41 and 42 could require court resolution.

rows.title: Proposition 41 · Special taxes and spending limit
rows.method: Could nullify conflicting taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026. Net fiscal effect depends on later decisions; read alongside Prop 40.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Add audits of new special-tax programs and restrict exclusions of new special-tax revenues from the state spending limit.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Could nullify conflicting taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026. Net fiscal effect depends on later decisions; read alongside Prop 40.

options.name: No
options.description: Keep current audit responsibilities and spending-limit requirements.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Add reviews and ongoing audits for programs funded by new special taxes, and restrict exclusion of new special-tax spending from the state spending limit. Audit and ballot-publication costs would rise.
rows.decision: Weigh additional review and spending constraints against administrative burdens and reduced flexibility to raise and spend earmarked revenue.

rows.title: Proposition 42 · Personal-property and retroactive taxes
rows.method: Could constrain future revenue and affect Prop 40. Personal property here includes financial assets and other non-real-estate property.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Prohibit new state personal-property taxes and specified retroactive taxes; nullify conflicting taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Could constrain future revenue and affect Prop 40. Personal property here includes financial assets and other non-real-estate property.

options.name: No
options.description: Retain the state’s option to establish such taxes.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Bar new state taxes on ownership of financial assets and other personal property, and certain retroactive taxes. The analyst says future revenue could be lower, with timing and size unknown.
rows.decision: Weigh limits on future taxation against keeping revenue options available. A conflict with Proposition 40 could depend on relative Yes votes and court interpretation.

rows.title: Proposition 43 · Local special-tax threshold
rows.method: Changes which future local taxes can pass; official analysis says future local revenues might rise less.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Raise approval for voter-proposed local special taxes from majority to two-thirds starting Jan 1, 2027.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Changes which future local taxes can pass; official analysis says future local revenues might rise less.

options.name: No
options.description: Retain majority approval for those voter-proposed taxes.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Require two-thirds approval for certain local taxes that can currently pass by majority vote. The analyst expects potentially lower future local revenue; the amount depends on future proposals and votes.
rows.decision: Weigh stronger supermajority protection for taxpayers against the ability of local majorities to fund services.

rows.title: Proposition 44 · Community-clinic spending rule
rows.method: Creates penalties and oversight; official state administration costs in the low tens of millions annually would be covered by fees.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Require specified nonprofit community clinics to spend at least 90% of annual revenue on program services.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Creates penalties and oversight; official state administration costs in the low tens of millions annually would be covered by fees.

options.name: No
options.description: Do not enact the new spending requirement.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Require certain private nonprofit safety-net clinics to spend at least 90% of revenue on health-care services. Enforcement fees would fund state oversight; compliance could change services or cause some clinics to close.
rows.decision: Weigh a direct-care spending floor against operating flexibility, reporting costs and the uncertain effects on access to care.

rows.title: Proposition 45 · Environmental review procedures
rows.method: Tightens deadlines and narrows court review. Initial public costs may exceed $100M annually, partly fee-funded; longer-term fiscal effects are uncertain.

options.name: Yes
options.description: Create faster review and court-challenge procedures for eligible projects, including many housing and infrastructure projects.
options.why: Adopts the proposed change. Tightens deadlines and narrows court review. Initial public costs may exceed $100M annually, partly fee-funded; longer-term fiscal effects are uncertain.

options.name: No
options.description: Keep existing review and court-challenge procedures.
options.why: Retains the current law or rejects the proposed authorization, as described above.

rows.office: Create new environmental-review and court-challenge procedures for eligible projects, including tighter time limits and limits on court review. The analyst expects significant initial administrative costs and uncertain longer-term effects.
rows.decision: Weigh potentially faster projects and lower project costs against changes to environmental scrutiny and the scope of legal challenges.
